title: Interpretation of Statutes
outcomes: Apply secondary rules and strict or beneficial construction.
Use internal and external aids and interpret deeds and documents.

meta.exam_tip: For problem questions, name the rule, state it in one line, apply it to the facts and conclude.

concepts.title: Statutes and why interpretation is needed
body: A statute is law enacted by Parliament or a State Legislature. Interpretation is the process by which courts find the true meaning of the words used and the legislature's intention; construction goes further, drawing conclusions about matters not directly covered.
Interpretation is needed because language is imperfect, situations unforeseen by the drafters arise, and words may have several meanings.
Statutes, deeds and documents are interpreted by the same broad approach: find the intention from the words used, read as a whole.
concepts.analogy: Interpretation finds what the law-maker meant from what the law-maker wrote.
concepts.work: Whether "computer" in an old Act includes a smartphone is a question of interpretation.

concepts.title: Primary rules: literal, mischief, golden and harmonious construction
body: Literal rule: words are given their plain, ordinary meaning. If the language is clear, the court applies it even if the result seems harsh; consequences are for the legislature.

Mischief rule (Heydon's case): the court asks what the law was before, what mischief it did not cover, what remedy Parliament provided, and the true reason for it — and reads the words to suppress the mischief and advance the remedy.
Golden rule: the literal meaning is modified only so far as needed to avoid absurdity, repugnancy or inconsistency.

Harmonious construction: where two provisions seem to conflict, they are read so that both operate; one should not be read to defeat the other. Where reconciliation is impossible, the specific provision prevails over the general.
concepts.analogy: Start with the words; depart only to avoid absurdity, conflict or defeat of the law's purpose.
concepts.work: A law against "drawing a weapon at a person" is read to include an unloaded gun because that was the mischief targeted.

concepts.title: Secondary rules: noscitur a sociis, ejusdem generis, reddendo singula singulis
body: Noscitur a sociis: a word is known by the company it keeps — a doubtful word takes colour from words around it.
Ejusdem generis: where general words follow specific words of a distinct class, the general words are limited to things of the same class. The rule applies only if the specific words form a class.
Reddendo singula singulis: where several words are used together referring to several subjects, each word applies to its matching subject.
Strict construction applies to penal and taxing statutes: any reasonable doubt is resolved in favour of the subject. Beneficial (welfare) laws are construed liberally in favour of those they protect.
concepts.analogy: Words are read with their neighbours and their class.
concepts.work: "Warehouses, shops and other places" in a licensing law refers to places of business, not private homes.

concepts.title: Internal aids to interpretation
body: Internal aids are found within the statute: long title and preamble (to understand purpose when words are unclear), headings of chapters and sections, marginal notes (limited weight), definitions and interpretation clauses ("means" is exhaustive; "includes" is extensive), illustrations, provisos (an exception carved out of the main enactment), explanations (clarify meaning), schedules, and punctuation (minor weight).
Internal aids help resolve ambiguity but cannot control clear words of the enacting provision.
concepts.analogy: Look inside the Act first — titles, definitions, provisos and illustrations.
concepts.work: A definition using "includes" enlarges the ordinary meaning rather than limiting it.

concepts.title: External aids and interpretation of deeds and documents
body: External aids come from outside the statute: parliamentary history (bills, statements of objects and reasons, debates, committee reports — used with care), historical background and earlier laws, later social, political and technological developments, dictionaries, foreign decisions on similar laws, textbooks, and other statutes on the same subject (in pari materia).

Deeds and documents are interpreted to find the intention of the parties from the whole document: plain meaning first; where words are ambiguous, the circumstances may be considered; where two clauses truly conflict, the earlier clause generally prevails in a deed, while in a will the later clause prevails (as the last expression of intention); specific words control general ones.
concepts.analogy: When the Act itself is unclear, its history and context can help.
concepts.work: Courts have used the Oxford dictionary to decide whether "manufacture" covers a process.

illustrations.title: Which rule applies?
illustrations.q: Apply the right rule: (a) A law taxes "cars, trucks, buses and other vehicles". Is a bicycle covered? (b) A law prohibits "sleeping on railway platforms". Is a passenger who dozes off while waiting for a late train guilty? (c) Two sections of the same Act appear to conflict. How should a court read them?

head: Situation
Rule
Likely answer
rows: (a) "other vehicles" after motor vehicles
Ejusdem generis — general words take the meaning of the specific class before them
Covers only motor vehicles; a bicycle is outside
(b) Dozing while waiting
Mischief rule / golden rule — read in light of the mischief aimed at (vagrants using platforms as beds)
Not guilty — the law targets those using platforms as sleeping places
(c) Apparent conflict
Harmonious construction — read both so each has effect
Reconcile them; avoid making either a dead letter

jobs.title: Advising on an unclear provision
jobs.situation: A client is unsure whether a new GST exemption covering "fruits, vegetables and other produce" applies to dried spices.
steps: Check the definitions and explanations in the Act.
Apply ejusdem generis and noscitur a sociis.
Look at the notification's purpose and any circulars.
jobs.takeaway: Use rules and aids together to support a reasoned view.

mcqs.q: The rule that gives words their plain and ordinary meaning is the:
mcqs.explain: The literal rule applies the ordinary grammatical meaning of words; if clear, it must be followed even if the outcome is harsh. Other rules come in only when literal reading fails. In practice: start here.
mcqs.topic: Primary rules: literal, mischief, golden and harmonious construction

mcqs.q: Heydon's case is associated with the:
mcqs.explain: Heydon's case laid down the mischief rule: identify the previous law, the mischief, the remedy and its reason, and interpret to suppress the mischief and advance the remedy. In practice: useful for remedial laws.
mcqs.topic: Primary rules: literal, mischief, golden and harmonious construction

mcqs.q: Where two provisions of the same Act appear to conflict, courts apply:
mcqs.explain: Harmonious construction reads both provisions so that each has effect; only if they cannot be reconciled does the specific one prevail over the general. In practice: avoid making a provision useless.
mcqs.topic: Primary rules: literal, mischief, golden and harmonious construction

mcqs.q: General words following particular words of the same class are limited to that class under:
mcqs.explain: Ejusdem generis limits general words to things of the same kind as the specific words they follow, provided those specific words form a genus. In practice: check that a class exists.
mcqs.topic: Secondary rules: noscitur a sociis, ejusdem generis, reddendo singula singulis

mcqs.q: "A word is known by the company it keeps" describes:
mcqs.explain: Noscitur a sociis says the meaning of a doubtful word may be found from associated words. It is broader than ejusdem generis. In practice: read lists as a whole.
mcqs.topic: Secondary rules: noscitur a sociis, ejusdem generis, reddendo singula singulis

mcqs.q: Taxing and penal statutes are generally construed:
options: Strictly, with doubt resolved in favour of the subject
Liberally in favour of the State
mcqs.explain: Because they impose burdens or punishment, taxing and penal laws are read strictly; reasonable doubt benefits the taxpayer or accused. Welfare laws are read liberally. In practice: check exemptions carefully.
mcqs.topic: Secondary rules: noscitur a sociis, ejusdem generis, reddendo singula singulis

mcqs.q: A definition clause using the word "means" is generally:
mcqs.explain: "Means" confines the term to the stated meaning; "includes" extends the ordinary meaning to cover more. In practice: read definitions closely.

mcqs.q: A proviso to a section normally:
options: Carves out an exception from the main provision
mcqs.explain: A proviso qualifies or excepts something from the enacting part that would otherwise fall within it; it does not usually expand the main provision. In practice: read it with the main section.

mcqs.q: Which is an external aid to interpretation?
mcqs.explain: The statement of objects and reasons and parliamentary debates come from outside the statute and are external aids; titles, illustrations and explanations are internal aids. In practice: use external aids with caution.
mcqs.topic: External aids and interpretation of deeds and documents

mcqs.q: The golden rule allows modifying the literal meaning to:
options: Give effect to the judge's view
mcqs.explain: Under the golden rule, the ordinary meaning is departed from only to the extent necessary to avoid absurdity, repugnancy or inconsistency with the rest of the statute. In practice: keep departures minimal.
mcqs.topic: Primary rules: literal, mischief, golden and harmonious construction

cases.title: The "places of entertainment" tax
cases.case: A State law levies tax on "cinemas, theatres, circuses and other places of entertainment". A municipal authority seeks to tax a public library that holds occasional book readings. The law is a taxing statute.

mcqs.q: The most relevant rule to read "other places of entertainment" is:
mcqs.explain: The general words follow a class of commercial entertainment venues, so ejusdem generis confines them to similar places. In practice: identify the common genus.
mcqs.topic: Secondary rules: noscitur a sociis, ejusdem generis, reddendo singula singulis

mcqs.q: Is the library likely to be taxable?
options: No, it is not of the same class as cinemas and circuses
Yes, any public place is covered
mcqs.explain: A library is not a commercial entertainment venue like the listed items; applying ejusdem generis and strict construction of taxing laws, it falls outside. In practice: doubt favours the taxpayer.
mcqs.topic: Secondary rules: noscitur a sociis, ejusdem generis, reddendo singula singulis

mcqs.q: As a taxing statute, any reasonable doubt is resolved:
options: By literal rule against the subject
mcqs.explain: Taxing statutes are construed strictly; if two views are reasonably possible, the one favouring the taxpayer is adopted. In practice: cite this principle in replies to notices.
mcqs.topic: Secondary rules: noscitur a sociis, ejusdem generis, reddendo singula singulis
